name: LMR62421XMFX_NOPB
title: SIMPLE SWITCHER 24 V output, 2.1 A step-up regulator, 1.6 MHz
summary: The LMR62421 is a 1.6 MHz current-mode boost regulator with a 2.1 A low-side NMOS switch, running from 2.7 V to 5.5 V and making outputs up to 24 V; it also serves as a SEPIC. Compensation and soft start are inside, the output is set by a divider to the 1.255 V feedback pin, and shutdown draws 80 nA. It comes in a 5-pin SOT-23 and a 6-pin WSON with exposed pad, and has cycle-by-cycle current limit and thermal shutdown.

circuits.title: Typical application
circuits.description: A boost converter from VIN up to an adjustable VOUT. L1 charges from VIN while the internal switch holds SW at ground and discharges through D1 into the output capacitor C2 once the switch opens. R2 over R1 brings VOUT down to the 1.255 V that FB regulates; C3 across R2 adds a zero to the loop for phase margin. R3 pulls EN up to VIN, so the converter runs whenever the input is present. C1 decouples the input.

operation.text: Fixed-frequency peak current-mode boost with a low-side NMOS switch. Each cycle starts on the falling edge of the oscillator's reset pulse, which turns the switch on: SW drops to about ground and the inductor current climbs linearly. A current-sense amplifier measures the switch current; that signal plus a corrective ramp is compared with the error amplifier output, which tracks the gap between FB and VREF. When the comparator trips, the switch stays off for the rest of the cycle and the inductor current flows through D1, so SW rises to VOUT plus the diode drop. The loop sets the duty cycle that holds VOUT.

The switch current is limited cycle by cycle, 2.1 A minimum and 3 A typical. This protects only the internal switch: a boost has the inductor and diode in series from input to output, so a short on the output can pass enough current to damage both.

A logic low on EN shuts the part down; quiescent current falls to 80 nA typical, and switch leakage can draw up to 1 µA more from the input. EN thresholds: above 1.8 V enables, below 0.4 V shuts down. EN must never go above VIN + 0.3 V and must not float.
The part starts switching once VIN rises past 2.3 V typical (2.65 V max) and stops when VIN falls below 1.9 V typical (1.7 V min).
The output switch is turned off when the junction passes 160 °C and stays off until the junction cools to about 150 °C.
At start-up the error amplifier's reference ramps up to 1.255 V over about 4 ms, so VOUT rises at a controlled, nearly linear rate and inrush current is reduced.

A smaller inductor is smaller physically but gives more input ripple current; a larger one gives less. Size it for 10 % to 30 % ripple at maximum load, and check that the peak current stays below the 2.1 A minimum current limit. The inductor's saturation rating need only cover the peak at the highest designed input current, not the 3 A typical limit: for a 1.5 A input current with a 1.75 A peak, rate it above 1.75 A. Saturation drops the inductance abruptly and upsets regulation. At 1.6 MHz ferrite cores keep core loss down, and lower DCR gives better efficiency.

The input capacitor keeps VIN from sagging on switching transients; its key ratings are capacitance, voltage, RMS current and ESL. 10 µF to 44 µF is recommended, depending on the application. At this switching frequency a high-ESL capacitor can have too much impedance for stable operation, so surface-mount parts are strongly recommended; multilayer ceramics in X7R or X5R suit both input and output. Check the capacitance that remains at the working voltage and temperature.

Ceramic output capacitors work without hurting transient response, and allow larger inductor ripple without much more output ripple. The output capacitor supplies the first part of a load step, so its impedance sets the size of the dip. With MLCCs the ESR is so low that the capacitive term dominates the ripple, which then looks roughly sinusoidal and lags the switching by 90°. A ceramic also bypasses switching-edge noise coupled through the inductor's parasitic capacitance, which a tantalum does not. Together with one other external part, the output capacitor sets loop stability; most designs need at least 4.7 µF, X7R or X5R, checked at the working voltage and temperature.

Compensation is internal, with one optional external zero: a capacitor across the upper feedback resistor. In the 5 V to 12 V, 500 mA example without it, crossover is acceptable but phase margin at 0 dB is only 22°; a zero placed just above crossover, at 8 kHz with 220 pF, lifts the margin to at least 45°. With the internal compensation, an external zero anywhere from 5 kHz to 10 kHz yields good transient response and phase margin at any input and output voltage. The internal gm amplifier contributes a pole at the origin. A gain and phase measurement of the actual design is always recommended.

Every boost has a right-half-plane zero. In most designs it sits well above crossover and barely affects stability; it becomes a concern with large inductance and high output current. Other poles and zeros from parasitics inside the part, the external parts and the board lie well above crossover.

Couple the ground ends of COUT and the PGND pin tightly, and take them to the ground plane through at least two vias; a two-layer board wants unbroken ground copper over its whole bottom side. FB is high impedance: keep its trace short and the feedback resistors close to the part, with the ground end of R1 as near as possible to the IC ground (pin 5 on the WSON). Keep the VOUT trace feeding R2 clear of the inductor and of every switching trace. VIN, SW and VOUT carry large AC currents and want short, wide traces, though wider traces radiate more; a shielded inductor reduces radiated noise. Keep all other parts close to the IC as well. TI application note AN-1229 (SNVA054) has more.

The part also works as a SEPIC, whose output can sit above or below the input with the same polarity, unlike the Cuk and buck-boost. That suits a single Li-ion cell, 3 V to 4.5 V, feeding a rail inside that range. The boost analysis largely carries over. In each cycle the volt-seconds across each inductor sum to zero and the charge into each capacitor equals the charge out. During the on time the switch carries IL1 plus IL2, and that sum must stay under the 2.1 A minimum current limit. The boost layout rules apply to the SEPIC too.

In the WSON the die sits on a copper die-attach pad exposed on the underside, with bond wires out to exposed contacts. For higher power, the board land may be extended into a dog-bone shape, copper running out from both ends of the pad; a larger ground plane and thermal vias reduce θJA.
